newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU monetary commissioner sees timely start for EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU monetary commissioner sees timely start for EMU.

text.p: The European Union's Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said on Wednesday he was certain that economic and monetary union (EMU) would start on time with no softening of the entry criteria.
"In my view there is not even the trace of a doubt" that January 1 1999 would be the start date, he told the German parliamentary committee on European affairs.
De Silguy said EU finance ministers had affirmed this in the past two years at their regular meetings in Florence, Madrid and Dublin.

A delay in the start date would have negative political as well as economic consequences, as it would require a renegotiation of the Maastricht Treaty, which has been ratified by 15 countries, de Silguy said.
"Europe would lose credibility vis-a-vis its citizens and the rest of the world," he said. "The January 1999 start date is just as important as the strict application of the criteria."
"A delay would be destructive, and would act counter to our aims" by putting upward pressure on interest rates and inflation, he said.
Europe also had no choice but to apply the convergence criteria of the Maastricht Treaty strictly. "That is the only way to make the euro strong and stable," he said.
He added he believed EMU would start with a meaningful number of participants, including Germany.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who presented his EMU convergence report to his European counterparts on Monday, had received their acknowledgment that German unification had put special strains on its debt level.
That did not mean the debt criterion would be bent for Germany, de Silguy said, but he believed Germany would meet the targets on the strength of its own efforts.

All countries that fulfil the criteria could participate in the euro. The judgment of the starting participants, to be made in one year, would be made solely on the basis of economic, not geographic considerations, he said.
Germany is believed to be keen to keep out southern EU nations, notably Italy, to bolster confidence in the euro.
The European Commission will make the decision next spring on the basis of 1997 economic data, but it will also review the nations' budget plans for 1998 to ensure that stability is long-lasting.
